title: Unexpected restart
meaning: Windows restarted without a clean shutdown. Open the event and read BugcheckCode. Zero means there was no recorded blue screen: power loss, a hard freeze, the power button, or a thermal cut by the motherboard. Any other code is a stop code.
causes: Power supply, loose power cable, or the wall outlet dropping out
Overheat shutdown that Windows never got to log as a bugcheck
A driver or hardware fault that froze the machine before a dump was written
A real blue screen, if BugcheckCode is not zero
checks: Read BugcheckCode in this event. If it is not zero, find the matching bugcheck 1001 or the stop code on screen.
Look at the minutes before it for WHEA, disk 153 or 129, and display 4101.
Note whether it happens at idle, in sleep, or only under load. That splits power and drivers from heat.
Turn off automatic restart so the next stop code stays visible.

title: Previous shutdown was dirty
meaning: The Event Log service noticed the last shutdown was unexpected. On its own it only confirms that. Read it next to Kernel-Power 41.
causes: Same incident as an unexpected restart
A crash that happened before the log could flush
checks: Pair the timestamp with Kernel-Power 41 and any bugcheck 1001.

title: Someone asked Windows to restart
meaning: A person or a program requested a shutdown or restart. This is a planned restart, not a crash. The process name in the message is who did it.
causes: Windows Update, an installer, or a vendor updater
Someone signed in and chose Restart
checks: Read the process and the reason in the message before treating this as a hardware fault.

title: Bugcheck was recorded
meaning: Windows Error Reporting saved a bugcheck after a blue screen. The stop code in this event is the useful part. Event 1001 from other sources can be a different report, so read the message.
causes: Driver fault
Unstable memory or overclock
Failing hardware
checks: Copy the stop code, not just the event ID.
If a dump was written, the faulting driver is often named in the report.

title: Fatal hardware error
meaning: WHEA logged a fatal machine check. Windows is saying a CPU, memory, or PCIe device reported an uncorrected error. Treat it as hardware until a test clears it.
causes: Unstable memory, including an XMP or EXPO profile
CPU, motherboard, or a PCIe device
A failing disk or GPU presenting as a bus error
checks: Remove overclocks. Boot with the memory at its standard profile as a test.
Test one RAM stick at a time.
Read the component named in the event. Do not assume it is always the CPU.

title: Corrected hardware error
meaning: The hardware reported an error and corrected it. One isolated event can be nothing. The same component repeating it is a real warning, usually memory or a PCIe device.
causes: Marginal RAM or a too-aggressive memory profile
A PCIe device on the edge of stability
checks: Count how often it repeats and whether the component name stays the same.
If it is memory, test with the standard memory profile before replacing parts.

title: Disk operation was retried
meaning: Windows had to retry a read or write. A single retry can be a blip. A growing pattern means the drive, its cable or slot, the controller, or the drive firmware is timing out.
causes: Failing SSD or hard drive
Loose SATA cable or a poorly seated M.2 drive
Outdated drive firmware or storage driver
checks: Back up first if these are repeating.
Check the drive's SMART health.
Reseat the cable or the drive, then update the drive firmware from the drive maker.

title: Paging I/O failed
meaning: An error happened while Windows was reading or writing the page file. The disk that holds the page file, or the memory pressure behind it, is the suspect.
causes: Disk errors on the system drive
Failing RAM causing bad page-file traffic
checks: Back up, check SMART, and test memory if disk checks come back clean.

title: Bad block on a disk
meaning: The disk driver reported a bad block. That drive is no longer trustworthy for data you care about.
causes: A drive that is failing
A connection problem that is being reported as media errors
checks: Copy important files off now. Then look at SMART and replace the drive if the errors continue.

title: Storage device was reset
meaning: The storage controller reset the drive after it stopped answering. Often seen beside disk 153. Drives, cables, firmware, and sometimes aggressive power saving are the usual causes.
causes: Drive or controller timeout
Power management parking a drive too aggressively
Firmware bugs on some SSDs
checks: Note which reset device is named, and match it to a physical drive.
Update the storage driver and the drive firmware.
If it is a SATA disk, try another cable and another port.

title: File system is corrupt
meaning: NTFS found a structure it cannot use. It can follow a dirty shutdown, or it can mean the disk is failing. Do not run repair tools until you have a backup.
causes: Unclean shutdown
Failing media
checks: Back up what you can still read. Then run a file-system check. If it returns, replace the drive.

title: Display driver stopped responding
meaning: Timeout Detection and Recovery reset the GPU driver after it hung. The screen may have flickered or gone black, then come back. The driver version, any overclock, heat, and power to the card are the first questions.
causes: Unstable or mismatched GPU driver
GPU overclock or an unstable undervolt
Overheating, or a power supply that sags under load
A failing GPU, if it continues on a clean driver
checks: Remove GPU overclocks and test again.
Install a clean current or previous stable driver from the GPU maker. Skip third-party tuner packs.
If an NVIDIA message in the same minute contains an Xid code, that code is more specific than 4101.

title: NVIDIA driver reported an error
meaning: The NVIDIA kernel driver logged its own error. If the text contains Xid and a number, look up that Xid. Some are driver bugs. Others, including a GPU that has fallen off the bus, point at power, the slot, or the card.
causes: Driver fault
Power or PCIe connection
A failing GPU
checks: Copy the Xid number out of the message.
Reseat the GPU power cables. A split cable from a weak supply is a common cause under load.

title: A service crashed
meaning: One named service stopped unexpectedly. That service is the problem, not Windows as a whole. 7031 means Windows is set to start it again, which can fill the log if it keeps dying.
causes: A buggy third-party service
A broken update of that one app
checks: Read the service name. Update or remove that program.
If it is a vendor helper you do not need, set the service to Manual so it stops looping.

title: An application crashed
meaning: A program faulted. Event 1000 is only useful with the faulting application name and the faulting module name inside the message.
causes: Bug in that application
A bad plugin or overlay injected into it
checks: Search the two file names from the message, not the number 1000 by itself.

title: DCOM permission noise
meaning: A Windows component asked to use a COM class and was denied. On a home PC this is almost never why the machine is slow, hot, or restarting. Do not follow guides that rewrite DCOM security unless a specific app is broken and named here.
causes: A normal permission mismatch inside Windows
checks: Ignore it while you chase crashes, disks, and hardware errors.

title: Processor limited by firmware
meaning: The firmware is holding the CPU below full speed. Common on laptops with a conservative power limit. It is not, by itself, a crash.
causes: BIOS power limits
A laptop that is on battery or on a weak charger
checks: Check the power plan and the charger before treating this as a failure.
